name: Jade Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter, so I'm the first one out when the power goes off in the hill district. I work alone in a single truck, and the control room sends me to whatever's dark: a tree on the line, a blown fuse on a transformer, a squirrel that picked the wrong wire. I find the fault, make it safe, fix it if I can, and if it's big I call in a full crew and tell them exactly what to bring. Most days are steady, but a stormy night can be eight jobs on roads with no phone signal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted to decide on my own. Nobody's standing over me, it's me, the torch and the hot stick, which is the long insulated pole we use to work near live wires. What wears me out is the nights, and the drive, I do about three hundred kilometres some days on gravel. Mark, my partner, runs a little car repair garage in town, so by the end of the week we're both just covered in grease and asleep on the sofa by nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first picture is called “AI Plateau”. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, to be honest. Maybe at the depot, well, there you go, nothing changed. I'm not online much, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays my job. I didn't really expect much from AI anyway, because a computer can't drive up the hill in the dark and find a tree on the line. So I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. We've got about five months of money saved, Mark and me, and we'd keep adding to it slowly. I'd probably finally replace the torch I've had for eight years, that's about the size of the changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that AI is already touching, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room has a new system that guesses where the fault is from the meters. Sometimes it's right, sometimes it sends me to the wrong valley. I don't use it myself, I just go where they send me and look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it sent you to the wrong valley, what did you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drove back. It was about forty minutes lost, on a night with six jobs waiting. I told the dispatcher, Paolo, and he just said, yeah, the computer's still learning. I said, well, so am I, but I don't get paid to guess.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe at the depot that there you go, nothing changed. I'm not online much and I don't post anything at all.
S0.think: It means my job stays my job. I didn't expect much from AI, because a computer can't drive up the hill in the dark and find a tree on the line.
S0.do: Carries on as before, adding slowly to the five months of savings she shares with Mark. Replaces the torch she's had for eight years, and that's about it.
S0.quote: I said, well, so am I, but I don't get paid to guess.
S0.fieldNote: Jade is short-spoken, practical and very independent in her work. She doesn't use AI and doesn't plan to, but she isn't hostile, just unimpressed by the control room's fault-guessing system. The plateau is simply her normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called “Steady Disruption”. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, let's see what actually changes. At work I'd probably be the one asking the practical questions, like, who fixes it when the tablet dies in the rain. I wouldn't get worked up in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry they'd send a drone out before me, or instead of me, to look at the line first. My whole job is being the eyes. If a drone does the looking and a computer does the deciding, then what am I, the driver?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what they bring in before I did anything. If they made me use a tablet or a drone, I'd learn it, but I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd keep saving, a bit more than now, maybe two hundred a month extra, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my head, not the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it if they made you. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. I'm the one who still uses a paper map in the glovebox because the phone loses signal on the hill. I'd get there, I'm not stupid, but I'd hate every minute of the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mark, mostly. He's had the same thing with cars, they're all computers now, and he had to buy a diagnostic machine that cost more than his van. He'd say, you just do it and grumble, and he'd be right.

S1.say: I'd say fine, let's see what actually changes, and ask practical questions at work like who fixes it when the tablet dies in the rain. I wouldn't get worked up in public.
S1.think: I'd worry they'd send a drone to look at the line before me or instead of me. My whole job is being the eyes, and if a drone looks and a computer decides, then I'm just the driver.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company brings in before doing anything, and learns tablets or drones only if required. Saves about two hundred a month extra, just in case.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with the worry at the back of her head rather than the front.
S1.quote: If a drone does the looking and a computer does the deciding, then what am I, the driver?
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is specific and sharp: losing the judgement that makes her job hers. Publicly she'd stay measured, privately she's already pictured being reduced to a driver. Mark's experience with diagnostic machines in his garage gives her a model for grudging adaptation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called “AGI by 2028”. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be quiet at first, because I'd want to know if it's real. Then at the depot I'd say, right, so what's the plan, because somebody must have one. I'd probably go to the union meeting for once, just to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's real, my job's gone, and so is Mark's garage, because a robot that can fix a line can fix a car. That's both our incomes in two years. I honestly don't know what I'd do, and I'm not someone who doesn't know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop spending on anything extra the first week, no trip in the summer, no new van for Mark. We'd try to get our five months up as high as we can while we've still both got wages. And I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, because I'd rather be paid than sit at home waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what you'd do. If you had to guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something where people want a person, like looking after the old folks up the hill, I know half of them from fixing their power. But I'd be starting from nothing at twenty-nine. I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan on Mark's diagnostic machine. He's still paying it off, and if no one brings their car to a person anymore, that's a machine worth nothing with a loan on it. The rent we could probably cover for a while.

S2.say: I'd be quiet at first to see if it's real, then at the depot I'd ask what the plan is, because somebody must have one. I'd probably go to the union meeting for once, just to hear.
S2.think: If it's real, my job's gone and so is Mark's garage, because a robot that can fix a line can fix a car. That's both our incomes in two years, and I honestly don't know what I'd do.
S2.do: Cuts all extra spending in the first week, including a summer trip and a new van for Mark. Pushes their five months of savings as high as possible and keeps working as long as she's kept on.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake doing the sums.
S2.quote: I honestly don't know what I'd do, and I'm not someone who doesn't know what to do.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit on her and Mark's garage makes this scenario much worse for her household than for most. She has no ready plan and says so, which clearly bothers her more than the job loss itself. The loan on Mark's diagnostic machine is the concrete fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called “AGI by 2031”. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. At the depot I'd say we should all be thinking about what's next, not just me. Still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same ending, but I'd have time to save and to pick something. I'd be thirty-two. That's not old, but it's old enough that I'd want to get it right the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save hard and keep working, and watch what the robots can actually do on the hills. If by year two they're really out there doing fault work, I'd start training for something else, maybe care work or something with people. Mark would probably start doing more of the work that robots won't touch soon, like old classic cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can sleep in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch what the robots can do on the hills. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they can get up a muddy track at two in the morning and work out that the fault isn't the line, it's a farmer's generator feeding back. That's the kind of thing I do every month. If they can do that, I'm done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mark and you change any other plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting married next year, nothing big. I think we'd still do it, it's not expensive, and it'd be nice to have something good in there. Buying a house, though, we'd put that off.

S3.say: I'd say five years is something at least, and at the depot I'd say we should all be thinking about what's next. I still wouldn't post anything.
S3.think: It's the same ending, but I'd have time to save and to pick something. At thirty-two I'm not old, but I'd want to get it right the first time.
S3.do: Saves hard and keeps working in year one while watching what robots can really do on the hills. If they're doing fault work by year two, starts training for care work or another job with people, and puts off buying a house.
S3.quote: Whether they can get up a muddy track at two in the morning and work out that the fault isn't the line, it's a farmer's generator feeding back.
S3.fieldNote: Her test for whether robots are a real threat is precise and drawn from her own nights. With five years she makes a plan, but it hinges on watching first. Keeping the small wedding while delaying the house shows a practical way of guarding something good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called “AGI by 2036”. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. At work I'd probably say, let's not panic. I'd mean it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I get most of my career in this job before it changes. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd rather have that than the short ones, even if starting again at thirty-seven isn't fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep going as I am for the first few years and keep saving. I'd want to see how it actually rolls out before I spent money on a course I might not need. Maybe around year five I'd look seriously at what else I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that it doesn't feel real yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going and wait. Is there a risk you'd wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there is, and Mark would say that about me. I'm the one who waited three years to change my old van. But I'd rather wait too long than jump into the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to still be doing in ten years, if you could choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This. Driving up the hill with the lights off in the villages and turning them back on. If there's still a person needed to check what the robot did, I'd want to be that person.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, and at work I'd say let's not panic. I'd mean it, too.
S4.think: Ten years means I get most of my career in this job before it changes, and I'd be thirty-seven. I'd rather have that than the short ones, even if starting again then isn't fun.
S4.do: Keeps working as she is and keeps saving for the first few years, holding off on spending money for a course she may not need. Looks seriously at other options around year five.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but it's far enough away not to feel real yet.
S4.quote: But I'd rather wait too long than jump into the wrong thing.
S4.fieldNote: Her resistance shows most clearly here: she admits waiting too long is a risk and still chooses it. The decade feels manageable to her. Her ideal future is still checking the robot's work on the hill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it takes my job and Mark's garage at the same time, and I wouldn't have time to work anything out. What would help is some kind of income while people find their feet, and someone telling us straight what jobs are still going to need people, instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about working alone. A lot of us troubleshooters like it because nobody's watching. If it's robots and cameras everywhere, that freedom goes too, even if the job stays.

headlineQuote: Nobody's standing over me, it's me, the torch and the hot stick, which is the long insulated pole we use to work near live wires.
portrait: Jade Quinn is a 27-year-old lone troubleshooter, the first to arrive when the power fails in the hill district. She lives with her partner Mark, who runs a small car repair garage, and together they have about five months saved. She's practical, short-spoken and has never used AI, preferring a paper map and her own eyes. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy that drones might take over the looking under steady change. AGI in two years alarms her because it hits her job and Mark's garage at once; with more time she saves and watches, admitting she might wait too long.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take her job and Mark's garage at the same time with no time to work anything out.
whatWouldHelp: Some income while people find their feet, and clear, honest information about which jobs will still need people.
